answers.stem_only: The primary is an alias record for an ALB, so turn on Evaluate Target Health on the primary alias record: Route 53 then treats the record as unhealthy when the ALB has no healthy targets and answers with the S3 secondary. No separate health check or script is needed (a Route 53 HTTP health check on the primary also works but adds a resource to manage).

On-premises servers resolving a private hosted zone need an inbound Route 53 Resolver endpoint in the VPC; the data center DNS servers conditionally forward corp.internal to the endpoint IP addresses over Direct Connect. The VPC+2 resolver is not reachable from outside the VPC.
A zone apex (example.com) cannot hold a CNAME, and ALB IP addresses change; create an alias record of type A at the apex that points to the ALB.

Add a geolocation record with location Default pointing to the us-east-1 ALB; it answers for every location without a matching record, including unidentified locations. Keep the Europe and North America records.

Rely only on the Route 53 data plane: pre-create failover records (primary us-east-1 ALB, secondary us-west-2 ALB) and make the primary's health come from a health check or Evaluate Target Health so failover happens automatically without any record change during the event. Hosted zones are global and cannot be moved; editing weights or creating records are control-plane actions.

The primary is a non-alias A record with an Elastic IP, so Evaluate Target Health is not available; create a Route 53 HTTP health check of the primary endpoint and associate it with the primary failover record. The secondary needs no health check.

VPC resources resolving an on-premises domain need an outbound Resolver endpoint plus a forwarding rule for onprem.corp whose targets are the data center DNS servers, with the rule associated with the VPC.
At the apex, create two alias records that point to the CloudFront distribution: one of type A (IPv4) and one of type AAAA (IPv6). No CNAME at the apex and no hard-coded IPs.

Create a Route 53 public hosted zone, recreate all the records there (ideally lower the old NS TTL first), then update the domain's name servers at the current registrar to the four Route 53 name servers of the hosted zone. Registration does not have to move.
Weighted alias records for the two ALBs (90/10), then change the weights over the week; set version 2 to weight 0 to roll back.
Latency-based alias records for the two ALBs, one per Region, with Evaluate Target Health so an unhealthy Region is skipped.

Lower the TTL of the A record well in advance (at least the old TTL of one day before the cutover) so cached answers expire; on the day switch the record to an alias for the ALB; the short TTL also allows a quick rollback.

When all health-checked records of a weighted group are unhealthy, Route 53 treats them all as healthy and keeps returning them. Add a fallback: a weighted record with weight 0 is considered only when every nonzero-weight record is unhealthy, so a weight-0 alias record for the S3 website endpoint (bucket named www.example.com) serves the error page. Alternative with more work: nest the weighted set under failover records with S3 as secondary.

Route 53 health checkers run on the internet and cannot reach private IP addresses. Publish a CloudWatch metric for the API's health, create an alarm on it, and create a Route 53 health check that monitors the alarm state; associate it with the primary record. No public IPs.
Geolocation routing: a Europe record that points to the eu-west-1 ALB and a Default record that points to the us-east-1 ALB.

Use ELB health checks on each Auto Scaling group so failed instances are replaced, and Route 53 failover alias records (primary us-east-1 ALB, secondary us-west-2 ALB) with Evaluate Target Health on the primary for Regional failover.

Split-view DNS: for a VPC associated with a private hosted zone, Route 53 Resolver answers the whole example.com namespace from the private zone and does not fall back to the public zone. Copy the public records that the VPC needs (api.example.com) into the private hosted zone.
Active-active latency-based alias records for the two ALBs with Evaluate Target Health = Yes, so users go to the lowest-latency healthy Region with no extra health checks to manage.

Move the public domain to a Route 53 public hosted zone (globally distributed authoritative DNS with a 100 percent availability SLA) and change the name servers at the registrar to the hosted zone's name servers.

ALB IP addresses change as it scales, so never hard-code them. Replace the A record with an alias A record to the ALB; alias queries to ELB are free, which makes it cheaper than a CNAME (charged queries).

Put a Network Load Balancer (TCP) in front of the six instances across both AZs and point an alias record to it; the NLB health checks stop new connections to a failed instance at once regardless of client DNS caching.

Cross-account private hosted zone association: in the zone-owner account run create-vpc-association-authorization (CLI/SDK/API, not the console), then from the workload account run associate-vpc-with-hosted-zone, then delete the authorization.
